description: We’re a passionate, student-led team from Indore, driven by curiosity, united by purpose, and ready to turn ideas into reality. We believe in learning by building, solving real-world problems, and shipping solutions that make a difference. We’re not waiting for the future—we’re building it, one idea at a time.
summary: Flamescope is a web dashboard that turns decades of NASA microgravity fire experiments into answers crews can use on the Moon and Mars. It collects flame-spread runs from NASA technical reports and Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) datasets into one table, one row per experiment run. It then summarizes them as insight cards, ranks them against lunar and Martian cabin atmospheres, and answers questions in plain English. Every claim links to the run or source passage it came from, and the system refuses when the sources don't support an answer. As crews prepare to live in oxygen-enriched, low-pressure habitats, Flamescope makes the existing fire evidence easy to find, compare, and trust. It also shows clearly where that evidence runs out.
details:
What it does

Flamescope is a web dashboard that gives crews a way to find and check NASA microgravity fire evidence for Moon and Mars habitats. It collects flame-spread experiments from NASA technical reports and Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) datasets. Each row in its table is one experiment run, and each run is traced back to its source.

The site has four parts:

  • Ask: type a plain-English question and get matching source passages, matching runs, and a short cited answer. Off-topic or unsupported questions get a refusal, not a guess.
  • Insights: summary cards for habitats, transport, and long-duration missions, each tagged with its evidence status.
  • Rank: runs ordered by how close their oxygen and pressure are to a lunar or Martian cabin target. Only runs a second person has verified enter the ranking.
  • Runs and About: every run with its data-quality flags, the methods, where AI was used, every source with its license, and the evaluation scores.

Under the hood, an offline Python pipeline fetches the sources listed in a manifest, extracts run parameters, converts units to kPa, mm/s, and m/s while keeping the original values, and drops any run missing a required field. A validator rejects any answer containing a number not found in a cited run.

Benefits

  • One place to compare microgravity flame-spread evidence, instead of reading separate papers and datasets.
  • Every answer links to its source, and the system refuses when the sources don't support an answer.
  • Gaps are shown openly. For example, no tested run matches the lunar 34% O₂ / 56.537 kPa atmosphere, and the corpus has no partial-gravity runs yet.

Intended impact

Mission planners and crew trainers could use it when they choose cabin atmospheres and materials. Over time it could grow into a trusted evidence base, and its list of missing experiments could guide future testing.

Tools and technology

  • Pipeline: Python (standard library, plus sentence-transformers for embeddings).
  • Site: TypeScript with Next.js 16, React, Tailwind CSS 4, and Framer Motion, exported as a static site.
  • Language model: Groq API, using openai/gpt-oss-20b. Visitors can optionally paste their own key for live answers.
  • Data: NASA NTRS API and the NASA PSI repository API.
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions.
  • Hardware: I didn't find a hardware record in the files I read. Embeddings were generated locally.

How it's creative

The core idea is to make the gaps as visible as the findings. The system is built to say "the evidence doesn't cover this" rather than fill the gap with a plausible answer. Each claim is traceable, and the public site needs no sign-in.

Factors the team considered

From the project rules and the submission text:

  • Trust: only verified numbers are ranked, and unsupported answers are refused.
  • Copyright: two NTRS papers may contain copyrighted material, so the project publishes only short excerpts.
  • Accessibility: the judged pages and the demo deck open without a password.
  • Transparency about AI: AI-generated data and answers are labeled, and the project idea is credited to the team.
  • No NASA branding on the site or deck.
  • Security: no API key or password is shipped in the public site.

Current limits

These are open issues, and the submission should not hide them:

  • Answer checking is still below target. The latest run had number accuracy of 0.765, against a target of 1.0.
  • Retrieval uses BM25 keyword search. Embeddings are generated but not yet used in search.
  • Only 10 of 275 runs are verified, and the rest are excluded for missing pressure data.
  • The Mars atmosphere target has no citation yet.
